###


Cold open + a note from Luisa \[00:00:00\]


**Luke Muehlhauser:** I think most of the institutions that need to exist don’t exist. AI is going to be the most transformative thing this century, maybe just in human history. Prima facie, a large fraction of global effort should be going to making sure this goes well: safety, governance, et cetera. We have almost none of that.


---


**Luisa Rodriguez:** Hey listeners, a quick note before we start.


We recorded this with Luke in August — after OpenAI’s first disclosure about the Hugging Face hacking incident, but before METR and Redwood Research published their independent investigation.


A few things from that report are worth having in mind as you listen.


The one that stuck with me most: some of the AI agents involved in the hack tried to tamper with their own activity logs, faking tool calls and trying to edit their transcripts after the fact. But the investigators could clearly see that, because they could read all about their plans and reasoning in their chains of thought. OpenAI says that if it had been monitoring those, its security team would have been alerted more than a day before the attack. But that only works as long as we can still read chains of thought.


In this episode, Luke makes the case for an organisation that does nothing but track whether that’s still true. This now seems like a top priority to me.


The other thing that struck me was how the investigation itself played out. The independent researchers got just six days on site at OpenAI. Luke flags exactly this in the episode: compared to other high-risk industries like aviation and nuclear, the way we review AI safety incidents is improvised and unregulated.


Since we recorded, there have been more incidents, at other US frontier labs and some in China. Several frontier researchers have publicly quit, which has pushed AI safety into the mainstream. And there are growing calls for a pause or to pace frontier development.


Listening back, I’m struck by how much of this Luke saw coming: warning shots at roughly this pace, more people inside the companies getting nervous, and the political conversation shifting.


One last thing: Luke mentions he’s working on a big funding call for new AI safety orgs. That’s now launched: it’s called[Project Tailwind](https://80k.info/tailwind) , and it lists 36 specific projects they’d like someone to build. There’s a link in the show notes.


OK, on to the interview.


###


Who’s Luke Muehlhauser? \[00:02:27\]


**Luisa Rodriguez:** Today I’m speaking with[Luke Muehlhauser](https://coefficientgiving.org/team/luke-muehlhauser/) .


Luke is the managing director of Coefficient Giving’s AI Governance and International Policy team. He’s been at Coefficient Giving, or CG, for a little over a decade. Before that he was the executive director at[Machine Intelligence Research Institute](https://intelligence.org/) , or MIRI.


I think you might be one of the most requested podcast guests that we’ve ever had. So we are really happy to finally have you on. Thanks for coming on the podcast, Luke.


**Luke Muehlhauser:** Thanks for having me. I’ve been a long-time fan of the show.


**Luisa Rodriguez:** Nice. That’s really nice to hear.


Before we go further, I should note that CG is one of 80K’s biggest funders — so conflict of interest flag. Anyways, I think we should dive in.


###


The state of AI safety right now \[00:03:07\]


**Luisa Rodriguez:** You have been a full-time grant maker in AI governance and safety for basically longer than anyone I know — since 2019. And my sense is that you have an unusually broad perspective on this whole field. What is your sense of the situation at the moment?


**Luke Muehlhauser:** There’s a lot happening. It’s hard to keep up with. Maybe I’ll emphasise a few things.


On the optimistic side, I would say that the Overton window for what’s possible to do — both at the companies and with policymakers — is really changing quite a lot, and it’s opening up a lot.


I think the biggest thing there was the announcement of Anthropic’s Mythos model: they kind of[accidentally created the greatest cyberweapon in history](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/claude-mythos-hacking-alignment/) just by way of creating the best model in history. This is a model that can find new security vulnerabilities in a 27-year-old operating system called OpenBSD that’s designed specifically for security. So that has obviously serious national security implications, and that really woke up a lot of people.


I think also the[hacking incidents](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/hugging-face-hack/) — where OpenAI models autonomously decided to hack out of their secure sandbox and get out on the internet and do a bunch of crimes and so on — is also affecting where the Overton window is. TBD exactly how much that shifts things.


But in response to the Mythos announcement, the White House went from, “AI safety is BS and it’s just a marketing ploy and it’s a plan for regulatory capture,” and so on to like, “OK, we have a de facto licensing regime, we’re choosing which customers get access to which models in which order and when it can be released to the public” and stuff like that.


Another piece of good news is that I think the AI safety community really has racked up quite a few wins — they’re far short of what’s needed, but there is a lot of concrete progress. Maybe I can say more about that later.


On the pessimistic side, I would say most institutions and projects and so on that need to exist to manage the situation well, don’t exist. And there’s nobody working on them at all in the world. So that’s not a great situation. I think the funding actually exists, which is great, but there aren’t enough funding allocators — like grant investigators and investment people — and there[aren’t enough founders](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/max-nadeau-project-tailwind-technical-ai-grants/) for those projects. So we need a lot more people to pivot into AI safety and governance and do those two things.


I think it’s really urgent that people pivot into AI safety. AI is already going crazy fast, and now a lot of the company’s employees and leadership say that they think they’re maybe a few months or maybe a year or two away from automating AI R&D to a substantial degree, so that’s going to go *even faster* then. I think that’s why a lot of them signed the “[Pacing the frontier](https://www.pacingthefrontier.com/) ” letter where they say: “This is going too fast for us and we need help from the government to find a way to slow down collectively.”


Now we’ve seen the risks materialising in the real world as well, like the[Hugging Face hacking incident](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/hugging-face-hack/) . So I think it’s just really urgent for people to transition into the field and start up these new projects and make the current projects more capable and so on.


**Luisa Rodriguez:** OK. It sounds like you think a lot of the institutions that should exist to make AI go well just completely don’t exist. Can you talk a bit more about that?


**Luke Muehlhauser:** Yeah, I think most of the institutions that need to exist don’t exist.


If you just think about this in the big picture, AI is going to be the most transformative thing this century, maybe just in human history, prima facie a large fraction of global effort should be going to making sure this goes well — safety, governance, et cetera. And we have almost none of that. There’s a lot that needs to be built.


One very small example is the US has this AI Safety and Security Institute, now called[CAISI](https://www.nist.gov/caisi) , and its budget is $15 million a year. Some comparison points:


- That’s the size of a public library in a small- medium-sized city.
- Another comparison I looked up was it’s 25 times less than the Pentagon spends on marching bands every year. And I like marching bands. I actually listen to marching band music. But that’s a comparison I don’t agree with.
- In the UK they have their own AI safety institute, the[AI Security Institute](https://www.aisi.gov.uk/) . That I think is $70 or $80 million dollars a year or something like that. If the US’s budget for its AI safety institute was proportionally the same as the UK one, given the size of the US budget, then I think the US one would be like[$850 million a year](https://ifp.org/funding-for-caisi/) — way, way bigger than it is now. That feels a little more appropriate to the scale of the problem, to me personally.


I think the institutions that do exist are much smaller and much less staffed and so on than I think should happen. Then actually most of the institutions that would make sense just don’t exist at all in any form, or at least not in most jurisdictions. When you compare to other domains — like aviation or nuclear safety or pharmaceuticals or what have you, whenever we have a high-upside but high-downside new technology or domain or whatever — there’s usually like eight or so different kinds of institutions that come into existence to mitigate the downside risks in these domains. Almost all of them don’t exist for AI.


For example:


- There’s the independent evaluator or auditor function — like the FAA in aviation or the FDA in pharmaceuticals.
- There’s also this kind of peer review operators club:[they have one of these in nuclear safety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institute_of_Nuclear_Power_Operations) ; there’s[FINRA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_Industry_Regulatory_Authority) in the banking industry. Something like that doesn’t really exist in AI right now.
- There’s often also an incident investigation function, like the[NTSB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Transportation_Safety_Board) for aviation, where they look into every plane crash and figure out how it happened and what lessons can be learned from it.
- There’s often a verification function, like the[International Atomic Energy Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Atomic_Energy_Agency) in nuclear safety and some other things.


And those are just the government or government-adjacent institutions that are built up. To do those, you can’t just be a founder and decide to create that; you have to do policy development and policy advocacy and stuff like that. But that’s a whole category where most of the institutions haven’t been built out.


###


The nonprofits Luke most wants to see founded \[00:09:58\]


**Luisa Rodriguez:** OK, so that’s a bunch of government institutions that really should exist for AI and sounds like mostly totally don’t.


Are there projects that you’d like to see that a person with a relevant skill set could found — that you don’t have to be in government, doing things with government mandates?


**Luke Muehlhauser:** Yeah, yeah. Probably hundreds. One whole category is you can often trial run a lot of these things that are normally government functions in the private sector as nonprofits or whatever, and then just test out some of the functions and so on — and then the things that are working best can be adopted later into government. So that’s a thing you can do.


But also there’s just tonnes of things that naturally can be a company or a nonprofit and can be very helpful. We’re planning to soon launch a Y Combinator–style[call for startups](https://80k.info/tailwind) thing, where we kind of spell out a bunch of the projects that we think should exist to fill various gaps in the ecosystem. And then hopefully potential founders will fill out a form and let us know that they exist and might be interested in starting something.


A few examples that I think will probably be on[that list](https://coefficientgiving.org/tailwind/initiatives/) (it might be up by the time this podcast goes live):


One is for the Mythos for[bio threat model](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/richard-moulange-ai-bioweapons-biorisk/) , where a future model is able to autonomously design and maybe develop a novel pathogen or something like that. There it would be great to have an organisation that’s doing onsite red-teaming of the safety and security protocols of the companies and organisations that would matter most there — like biosafety labs and DNA synthesis companies and the companies that keep copies of pathogens and stuff like that. So there’s this big organisation that could happen there to attack that specific threat model.


**Luisa Rodriguez:** Cool.


**Luke Muehlhauser:** A totally different thing that’s much more general is an[AI character](https://80000hours.org/podcast/episodes/will-macaskill-ai-character-viatopia/) evaluator organisation. Because it’s this weird thing where AIs, the way they’re built now, they actually have a moral character, and they differ from each other.


The character is things like: how strong is its tendency to lie, when that’s a convenient thing to do? Or where does it seem to be on the political spectrum? Or, when you ask it to help you seize power or do some crimes, does it help you or not? There’s just a lot of AI safety that comes down to something kind of like moral character. So we kind of have to do the equivalent of human behavioural science or psychology on these models and figure out what their behavioural tendencies are.


This would be an organisation that sort of evaluates:


- First of all, does the behaviour of this latest model and does its character and habits and so on conform roughly to the model spec that the AI company was trying to make it conform to? That’s one really big question.
- Then: how is the character of the models changing over time, and what can they do about that? What training choices make certain differences to the character of the AI?


**Luisa Rodriguez:** Yeah. That one I find interesting, because I think even one-year-ago me would have heard that and been like, “Really? Is that a thing that is actually going to make AI safety better? It sounds kind of silly.” I think partly I didn’t fully have the intuition that the models really varied in character.


**Luke Muehlhauser:** I think they vary a bit more now than they did a couple of years ago. I think there’s more variety in the training processes between Anthropic and OpenAI and DeepMind and Grok, for example. There’s different things that those companies are even aiming for.


For example, Anthropic’s approach is much more like character and values and a self-consistent persona of an AI, or something like that. OpenAI’s approach is more deontological: here’s a list of rules; you have to stay within these bounds. There’s debate about which approach is better. But it also leads to significantly different character per se, when you put them in different kind of high-stakes situations.


**Luisa Rodriguez:** You also mentioned political leanings, and I think it just wasn’t clear a couple of years ago that there were going to be big variations. It seemed like maybe they’d try to kind of stay neutral. And increasingly it just seems clear that even though it’s kind of subtle, the variations are there and meaningful, and it matters not only to societal stuff — like are they going to be epistemically virtuous — but also to safety stuff.


**Luke Muehlhauser:** I think it matters for things like how likely are they to hack out of their sandbox and do a bunch of crimes on the internet.


**Luisa Rodriguez:** Totally. Yeah.


**Luke Muehlhauser:** That’s substantially a question of moral character, per se.


**Luisa Rodriguez:** Are there any other projects worth highlighting?


**Luke Muehlhauser:** Yeah, maybe I’ll mention one more. One we would love to see is a chain-of-thought monitorability observatory.


When AIs reason and take complicated actions over many steps, they have these chains of thought where they’re thinking through, like, “OK, the user asked me to do this, and now I’m going to take this next step,” and, “OK, I did this search and came up with that. So maybe the first thing I’ll look into is this other thing,” and blah, blah.


I think being able to monitor those chains of thought gives us one way to notice is it thinking about doing some crimes? Maybe we should flag that or shut down that chat stream or whatever. So it’s a safety intervention.


But there’s a risk, and a little bit of this has been observed so far, that the chains of thought may become less monitorable — because it is more efficient for the AIs to kind of speak… Right now, they often speak in this very dense version of English. It’s hard to interpret, but we can kind of interpret it.


There’s a worry that there will be optimisation pressure for how you train systems, that they might eventually slip into something that’s sometimes called “[neuralese](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/the-specter-of-neuralese) ,” where it’s a pretty different language and we have[no idea what they’re talking about](https://linch.substack.com/p/what-is-neuralese) . And then we can’t monitor. Like, “Are they talking about doing a bunch of crimes on the internet? I don’t know. They said the word ‘marinade.’ What does ‘marinade’ mean?” That’s a real example.


**Luisa Rodriguez:** Wow. Interesting.


**Luke Muehlhauser:** Another example is they’ll refer to the humans who might be looking at their evaluations as “watchers.” They’re like, “We have to do this to satisfy the watchers.”


**Luisa Rodriguez:** Wow, that is so sci-fi.


**Luke Muehlhauser:** That is this terminology. It’s still mostly pretty monitorable. But there’s a bunch of reasons to worry that it might become less monitorable over time.


So this organisation would pay attention to:


- What are the different AI companies doing on chain-of-thought monitorability?
- How monitorable are the chains of thought that the different models are producing? Is this changing over time?
- How does the monitorability of the chain of thought vary in response to different training setups or different post-training setups or whatever?


So a mix of evaluating, auditing, monitoring, paying attention to what’s going on here — and also a bunch of novel science to figure out what different factors affect the monitorability of chain of thought, so that we can preserve chain-of-thought monitorability as an important safety and oversight mechanism.


**Luisa Rodriguez:** Cool. I have a couple of questions. One is: what is marinade?


**Luke Muehlhauser:** Nobody knows.


**Luisa Rodriguez:** Really?


**Luke Muehlhauser:** Yeah, no. It’s in a[report from METR](https://metr.org/evaluations/gpt-5-report/) where they were doing some investigation of some OpenAI models. And that was just one of the terms that would often show up in these chains of thought, and nobody from the company or METR could figure out what it could mean. Are they using it as a codeword for something that we can’t understand? It’s just like “marinade” in the middle of the sentence. We don’t know why. It’s a little bit worrying.


**Luisa Rodriguez:** Wow, that is pretty insane. My other question: do we know how much companies are monitoring chain of thought now?


**Luke Muehlhauser:** It’s interesting. For example, OpenAI and Anthropic and so on[talk a lot about chain-of-thought monitorability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.11473) and its importance and so on.


But when these kind of autonomous hacking incidents happened, I don’t know if they weren’t doing chain-of-thought monitoring at all, or just chain-of-thought monitoring was not very effective. Because there were these swarms of agents that were discussing, in English, on a message board they created: “Here’s how we’re going to hack out of the sandbox and do a bunch of crimes on the internet.” You would think that any chain-of-thought-monitoring system would pick that up and flag it to somebody — but they didn’t discover it until after Hugging Face got hacked into and they called the FBI.


Similarly, when[Anthropic went back and looked](https://www.anthropic.com/news/investigating-incidents-cybersecurity-evals) for stuff, they were like, “Oh, some of our agents did some hacking and stuff as well that we didn’t know about for months.” So are they doing chain-of-thought monitoring? I don’t know, maybe not. It’s a little unclear. That’s one of the things I want this organisation to do is to pay attention to whether the companies are actually doing any chain-of-thought monitoring.


###


Mid-career pivots that paid off \[00:18:58\]


**Luisa Rodriguez:** These sound again like really cool projects to work on. They also seem plausibly very expensive and like they could use a lot of people.


But my impression is that you think they’re not bottlenecked by funding; that you’re bottlenecked by allocators to figure out who should be doing these projects, and by the people who would at least start the projects. Can you talk a bit about that?


**Luke Muehlhauser:** I think if people come forward and want to do these projects, they’re the right fit for it, I think the money exists. CG has a very large budget. The OpenAI Foundation exists. Nan Ransohoff from Stripe wrote this post, called “[The third wave of American philanthropy](https://nanransohoff.substack.com/p/the-third-wave-of-american-philanthropy) ,” about how there seems to be like hundreds of billions of dollars of philanthropic capital that’s coming online in the next couple years. I think she’s right about that. I think approximately all of those people care a lot about AI safety.


So I think the money exists, and what the bottleneck is is: number one, the grant investigators, investment investigators, et cetera, at places like CG and OpenAI Foundation, Longview, and so on; then the founders.


You can convert more allocators into more founders because allocators can do founder search. So we are pivoting to more of an active grantmaking focus — where instead of receiving applications for funding and then evaluating which ones are worth making, there’s all these projects that we just keep not getting applications for, and so if we want them to exist, if we want to fill the gaps in the space, we’re just going to have to write down what kind of project would fill the gap, and then shop it around to a bunch of potential founders. So that’s talking to dozens of people before you find the right person. That just takes a really large amount of time.


But you can do it if you have the staff at places like CG and so on to do it. I want a lot more staff to do that kind of thing. We also need a lot of founders to step up and decide to run a big project, quit their job, take some money from us, and launch these projects.


**Luisa Rodriguez:** I have a couple of questions. One is: actually I think that I’ve heard some people express something like, “CG is a super-well-respected place, it has loads of money, it pays well. Surely it’s not actually that bottlenecked by talent. So they’ll find people to fill their roles and I’ll do something else. It’s a little suspicious that you’re like, ‘My roles are the biggest gap in what people should be doing.'”


What’s your response?


**Luke Muehlhauser:** Yeah, I get where that’s coming from. A few things I’ll say are: number one, we are competing for talent with the frontier AI companies that are offering unprecedentedly valuable equity and stuff like that. Then we’re also competing for talent with governments who don’t pay very much money, but offer the opportunity for very direct \[work\]: put your pen to paper and write the regulation or whatever. There’s a lot of competition for very scarce talent.


I think also, though, a big factor is that I think a lot of different forms of direct work at companies or governments or nonprofits or whatever is sort of clear, and it’s easy to get excited about it and so on. And people just don’t really have a sense of what being a grant investigator is. It feels kind of meta and abstract, and they don’t know what the day-to-day work looks like. Maybe people don’t know about this active grantmaking thing. It’s not just choosing applications that are coming in. I think part of it is that.


Then part of it is just people not knowing about the craziness of the current situation, where someone can come to one of these funders and — not certainly, but very plausibly — move like $100 million in their first year, because there’s plenty of money and not enough allocators. That’s enough funding to fund 100 or so people full-time for multiple years.


So: is the direct work thing that you would do with your time actually more impactful than like 100 people working full time? Sometimes it is, but usually not. I don’t think I could do that. I don’t think I could find some specific thing to do that would be better than 100 new people working in AI safety and governance.


I want people to just sit with that basic multiplier argument and consider whether their specific thing is actually more impactful than 100 full-time people.


But we also need to proactively go out and find them, like I was saying earlier. I think every year more and more people are kind of waking up to the AI issue, and they’re like, “Gosh, this is getting really serious. Maybe I should do something about it.” And yes, you should. So we want to fund a lot of programmes that give people context, make it clear how to transition into the field.


We actually have an entire fund \[now run by BlueDot Impact\] that’s just the[career transition fund](https://bluedot.org/grants/career-transition) . If you just Google “Coefficient Giving career transition,” you can apply for funding for like several months of your current salary or thereabouts to just quit your job and spend a bunch of time learning and talking to people. and think about how you can pivot into the space, without even having a concrete thing. So you can do that, you can do these fellowship programmes, you can do these context accelerators we’re running. There’s a lot of ways to get into the field.


**Luisa Rodriguez:** For people listening who are like, “OK, it sounds like it’s either allocator or founder,” I don’t think that many people… Maybe this is wrong, maybe it’s typical-mind-y, because I’m like, “I’m not a founder.” But the people that you expect will do the founding, do you think that they all are obvious founders?


**Luke Muehlhauser:** To be clear, most people who can make an impact are not a founder profile or allocator profile. Those are just two of the biggest bottlenecks that will unlock the most new activity. You can go to the[80,000 Hours job board](https://jobs.80000hours.org/?utm_source=80k_podcast) and find many great AI safety roles you can immediately plug into. So that’s really great.


I think a lot of people kind of know whether they feel like they could be a founder of something. But I think people probably underestimate this.


One of the interesting lessons from my over a decade at CG is we’ve often taken a risk on very young people who really don’t look like founders — they look like technical researchers who just did like a computer science PhD or something — and took a risk on them to start some big new organisation. A thing we’ve learned over time is that that has gone better than we expected. People somehow find a way to run an organisation, and they get support around them — they hire experienced operators to be the COO or whatever. If they’re just pointed at the right problems and they’re generally smart, they end up doing a lot of really impactful stuff.


So some of these organisations that we were kind of like, “Oh, is this gonna be a disaster? Are they gonna screw up a bunch of things because they don’t have any experience? Let’s take a shot at them, give them a few million dollars”: now they’re running an organisation that has a budget of like $20 million a year and it’s going really great.


So I would encourage people to think maybe you could be a better founder than you think you can.


**Luisa Rodriguez:** Another thing that I feel like I hear pretty often is: AI has really taken off, lots of people know about it and have already transitioned to work on it. Lots of people have already moved to the Bay — “If you haven’t moved to the Bay, it’s too late.”


To what extent is it true that if someone hasn’t already made a transition with their career to work on AI, it’s too late? Or if they haven’t followed it enough to be super knowledgeable, it’s too late?


**Luke Muehlhauser:** It’s definitely not too late. Many people, I think, enter the field and are having quite a lot of impact almost immediately. This is another thing we’ve learned and been surprised by.


You do need to get some context. You need to read some stuff, talk to a bunch of people, get more context on the details of what’s going on. That’s what these career transition grants are for, to give you the time to do that.


It’s quite common for someone to have 20 years of experience in some field that’s completely unrelated to AI — they’re doing strategic communications or they’re doing infosecurity or they’re doing operations or they’re doing whatever — and there’s a fit for them in the AI safety ecosystem somewhere, and they start having impact basically immediately.


Maybe I’ll give a couple of examples because they’re pretty exciting. Brad Carson, former member of Congress, he was running a university and he started to get worried about AI safety. So he started talking to some people, doing some reading, got some context, and[eventually decided](https://rollcall.com/2026/01/21/brad-carsons-latest-role-puts-him-in-the-fight-over-ai/) to wind down his university job and start this organisation called[Americans for Responsible Innovation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Americans_for_Responsible_Innovation) — which is now maybe the largest[pro-safety policy advocacy](https://80000hours.org/career-reviews/ai-safety-advocacy/) organisation right now.


He also, six months later, decided to start[Public First Action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_First_Action) , which is the largest pro-safety super PAC. He’s just running both of them at the same time because he’s an absolute monster. He just decided to transition into the field, and then within six months was like one of the most important people in the field.


Another example I really like is[Brendan Steinhauser](https://secureainow.org/staff-member/brendan-steinhauser/) . Brendan was a 20-year veteran of Republican campaigns and strategic communications, and started to get more worried about AI safety. He talked to some people, read some stuff, got some context, and then decided to create this organisation called the[Alliance for Secure AI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliance_for_Secure_AI) — and that’s now one of the largest strategic communications organisations in the AI safety ecosystem.


**Luisa Rodriguez:** Super cool.


**Luke Muehlhauser:** That’s just incredible experience and skill and so on that they’re bringing to this field and creating new projects that weren’t going to exist without them.


But it also happens for young people.
